articles.title: Inside Health - The rise of robot-assisted surgery - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Can robots make surgery better for patients? And is it cost-effective?
articles.body: If you need an operation in the future, there's a good chance a robot could be involved. Around 70,000 robot-assisted surgeries are performed every year in England. But the plan is for that number to grow to half a million surgeries by the year 2035. In the recent budget, the UK government announced £100 million would be spent speeding up the rollout of robots across operating theatres in England. Those in favour say it is better for patients and surgeons – but why is that and how strong is the evidence? And with robotic systems costing millions of pounds, is this a good use of NHS funds? Laura Foster dons her scrubs and is invited into an operating theatre at Southmead Hospital in Bristol to witness a robotic surgery and speaks to surgeons and patients about how it works. Then a panel of experts, including Nuha Yassin from the Royal College of Surgeons England, Professor John McGrath from the NHS England Robotic Surgery steering committee and general practitioner and director of the Centre for Evidence and Values in Healthcare at St Andrews University, Dr Margaret McCartney, discuss the pros and cons of the technology. Presenter: Laura Foster Producer: Imogen Harper and Gerry Holt Editor: Ilan Goodman Sound engineer: Mary Stone Production coordinator: Stu Laws The show was made by the BBC Audio's Science Unit in collaboration with The Open University.

articles.title: Acidente na PA-419 em Prainha: Mulher morre e 7 ficam feridos | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente com caminhonete ocorreu perto do aeroporto da cidade. Vítima chegou a ser socorrida, mas morreu no hospital; duas pessoas estão em estado grave.
articles.summary: O acidente na PA-419 em Prainha causou a morte de uma mulher e deixou sete feridos após o pneu de uma caminhonete estourar e o veículo capotar diversas vezes na pista.
articles.body:
Veículo capotou após problema em um dos pneus. — Foto: Blog do Miranda

Uma mulher de 56 anos morreu e outras sete pessoas ficaram feridas após o capotamento de uma caminhonete Fiat Strada na tarde deste domingo (8), na rodovia PA-419, em Prainha, no oeste do Pará. O acidente aconteceu por volta das 13h40, nas proximidades do aeroporto do município.

A vítima foi identificada como Marinalva Santos da Silva Rodrigues. Ela chegou a ser socorrida por testemunhas e levada para o Hospital Municipal Wilson Ribeiro, mas não resistiu aos graves ferimentos e morreu cerca de uma hora após dar entrada na unidade de saúde. A morte foi confirmada pelo marido de Marinalva, Basílio Carvalho.

As outras sete pessoas que também viajavam no veículo sofreram ferimentos e foram encaminhadas para o mesmo hospital. Devido à gravidade das lesões, duas das vítimas aguardam transferência de emergência para o Hospital Regional do Baixo Amazonas, em Santarém.

Testemunhas que passavam pelo local no momento do acidente relataram que o pneu dianteiro da caminhonete estourou, fazendo com que o motorista perdesse o controle da direção. Na sequência, uma das rodas traseiras se soltou do eixo e o veículo capotou várias vezes na pista.

A Polícia Civil de Prainha vai instaurar um inquérito para apurar as circunstâncias e as responsabilidades do acidente. O corpo de Marinalva foi liberado para os procedimentos de velório e sepultamento no município.

articles.title: Policiais auxiliam mulher em trabalho de parto em via pública no Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: Após o parto, mãe e bebê foram encaminhadas ao hospital da cidade e passam bem.
articles.summary: Após o parto, mãe e bebê foram encaminhadas ao hospital da cidade e passam bem.
articles.body:
Policiais militares auxiliaram uma mulher que entrou em trabalho de parto em via pública no Bairro Zezinho Costa, em Várzea Alegre , no interior do Ceará, na noite deste sábado (7). A ação foi registrada por uma câmera de segurança. (veja o vídeo acima)

Conforme a Polícia Militar, por volta das 23h30, os agentes do Batalhão de Policiamento de Rondas de Ações Intensivas e Ostensivas (BPRaio) estavam realizando patrulhamento na Rua Figueiredo Correia quando foram abordados por um homem que pediu ajuda para a companheira grávida, que estava caída na pista, ao lado de uma motocicleta.

"Ao se aproximarem, os policiais foram informados de que ela estava grávida e, durante a avaliação inicial, constataram que já estava em trabalho de parto", disse a PM.

Durante a ocorrência, a mulher teve o bebê na rua, auxiliada pelo pai da recém-nascida.

"A criança nasceu com o cordão umbilical enrolado no pescoço. Os policiais retiraram o cordão e prestaram os primeiros cuidados à recém-nascida, que apresentava sinais vitais e chegou a chorar", informou a corporação.

Após o parto, a equipe levou a mãe e a bebê na viatura até o Hospital São Raimundo Nonato, onde as duas foram atendidas.

"Conforme o relatório da ocorrência, as duas estão em bom estado de saúde", falou a PM.

articles.title: Acidente na BR-040 em Levy Gasparian deixa motorista ferido | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu por volta das 13h30, na altura do km 3, na pista sentido Juiz de Fora (MG).
articles.summary: Um acidente na BR-040 em Levy Gasparian deixou um motorista ferido e geradores espalhados na pista sentido Juiz de Fora, provocando interdição parcial no km 3.
articles.body:
Motorista fica ferido após reboque com dois geradores perder o controle na BR-040, em Levy Gasparian — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

Um motorista ficou ferido após perder o controle de um caminhão que transportava dois geradores na tarde desta segunda-feira (9), na BR-040, em Levy Gasparian (RJ).. O acidente aconteceu por volta das 13h30, na altura do km 3, na pista sentido Juiz de Fora (MG).

Segundo a concessionária que administra a rodovia, com o impacto do acidente, os equipamentos caíram na pista.

O condutor foi socorrido por ambulância da concessionária e encaminhado ao Hospital Nossa Senhora da Conceição, em Três Rios (RJ), com ferimentos moderados.

Até o momento da publicação desta reportagem, o trecho estava sinalizado e operava em meia pista, aguardando a chegada da empresa responsável pela remoção dos geradores. Apesar da interdição parcial, não havia retenção no local.

articles.title: Jovem de 22 anos morre oito dias após cair de parapeito em bar no DF | G1
articles.standfirst: João Ricardo Damasceno era guitarrista de uma banda, estudante de cinema e fotógrafo. Morte foi confirmada pela banda Aurora neste domingo (8).
articles.summary: A morte de jovem em bar na Asa Sul foi confirmada após João Ricardo Damasceno, de 22 anos, passar oito dias internado com traumatismo craniano em Brasília.
articles.body:
João Ricardo Damasceno, de 22 anos, morreu após sofrer uma queda no Âmbar, na Asa Sul (DF). — Foto: Redes sociais

O jovem João Ricardo Damasceno , de 22 anos, morreu após cair de uma área elevada do bar Âmbar no Setor Bancário Sul, na Asa Sul, em Brasília .

A morte foi confirmada no sábado (7) e anunciada neste domingo (8) pela banda Aurora, na qual ele tocava guitarra. "Ric", como era conhecido pelos amigos, também era estudante de cinema e fotógrafo.

"Te amamos muito meu amigo e esperamos que de onde quer que você esteja, esteja feliz e em paz. Vamos viver por você e em memória a você. Obrigada por todo seu amor e dedicação. Você sempre estará vivo em nossa memória e em nossos corações", escreveu o perfil da Aurora.

A banda descreveu João Ricardo como um "amigo insubstituível e grande guitarrista" .

A mãe de João Ricardo também publicou uma homenagem ao filho nas redes sociais. Na mensagem, ela destacou a paixão dele pela fotografia e pela música e disse que se conforta ao saber que ele marcou positivamente a vida de tantas pessoas.

"Este é o meu maravilhoso filho, que partiu para brilhar no Reino do Céu. Meu fotógrafo, meu guitarrista, meu filho amado", escreveu.

"Obrigada, filho, por sua existência, e agora tire lindas fotos aí e alegre o Céu com sua guitarra bem tocada. Sua família tem muito orgulho de você! E você está aqui conosco todos os dias!", completou.

O velório de João Ricardo Damasceno ainda não foi marcado.

Âmbar em Brasília — Foto: Redes Sociais/reprodução

O acidente aconteceu em 31 de outubro. A ocorrência foi atendida pelo Corpo de Bombeiros do Distrito Federal. Segundo os bombeiros, o jovem estava inconsciente e apresentava suspeita de traumatismo cranioencefálico. Ele ainda sofreu uma parada cardiorrespiratória no local.

Após o atendimento, João Ricardo foi transportado pelo Samu para o Hospital de Base do Distrito Federal.

Na ocasião, o Instituto de Gestão Estratégica de Saúde do Distrito Federal (IgesDF) informou que o paciente havia recebido atendimento da equipe de trauma do pronto-socorro e permanecia internado sob os cuidados da equipe multiprofissional.

Uma pessoa que estava no local durante o fato contou ao g1 que havia um parapeito na área onde ocorreu a queda e que não viu nenhuma estrutura adicional de contenção ou bloqueio no local. Segundo o relato, o espaço estava cheio no momento do episódio.

Ainda de acordo com a testemunha, após a queda, o local onde aconteceu o acidente foi isolado com divisórias, mas a festa não foi interrompida.

articles.title: Mortes por dengue no Triângulo Mineiro: Homens são as maiores vítimas | G1
articles.standfirst: Em 2026, homens representam 63% do total de mortes pela doença; falta de cuidado pode aumentar gravidade.
articles.summary: Pacientes masculinos de 50 a 59 anos com comorbidades lideram óbitos por dengue no Triângulo Mineiro, evidenciando o risco de adiar a busca por socorro médico.
articles.body:
Homens de 50 a 59 anos são as principais vítimas de morte por dengue no Triângulo Mineiro e Alto Paranaíba , de acordo com o Painel de Monitoramento de Arboviroses de Minas Gerais. Somente neste ano, 7 morreram pela doença. O número é 63% do total de mortes, que foram 11, considerando os meses de janeiro a outubro.

Outras faixas etárias também tiveram mortes. É o caso de 1-9 anos, 40-49 anos, 60-69 anos, 70-79 anos e 90 anos ou mais, somando uma morte cada uma.

O cenário é o mesmo em relação à chikungunya. 60% das mortes pela doença são de homens. Nenhuma morte por zika foi registrada no período.

O infectologista Henrique De Villa Alves analisa que é necessário um estudo epidemiológico para saber o motivo das mortes, mas o hábito de cuidado é um indicativo.

“Geralmente as mulheres procuram mais os serviços de saúde. Os homens acabam ficando em casa e os números permitem a gente pensar que o homem acaba procurando a assistência médica justamente quando ele está mais grave”, explica.

Mosquito Aedes aegypti, causador da dengue — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

A região do Triângulo Mineiro e Alto Paranaíba concentra 36% do total de casos confirmados de dengue em Minas Gerais. São 17.941 dos 48.723 casos.

Em 86% os confirmados também são homens. Mulheres foram 13,9%.

O levantamento considera as macrorregiões de saúde Triângulo do Sul, Triângulo do Norte e Noroeste. Essa é uma estratégia da Secretaria de Estado de Saúde que agrupa municípios vizinhos e organiza pelo Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) para planejar, coordenar e garantir o acesso da população a serviços de média e alta complexidade (como hospitais de referência, UTIs, cirurgias e exames especializados).

No recorte de pessoas que morreram por conta da dengue, 63% morreram com comorbidades, como hipertensão, diabetes, doença renal e hepatopatias. A principal faixa é a de 50-59 anos.

Ainda segundo o médico Henrique De Villa Alves, isso evidencia a necessidade de não demorar para procurar atendimento.

“As comorbidades acabam sendo um agravante em mulheres com idade mais avançada. É importante procurar o serviço de saúde o mais rápido possível quando se desenvolve os sintomas de dengue. Sem tratamento, independente do sexo, existe chance de evoluir com gravidade, principalmente pacientes que têm comorbidades”, destaca.

articles.title: Motociclista fica ferido após ter pescoço atingido por linha com cerol | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso aconteceu na Avenida Afrânio Peixoto, no bairro do Lobato. Helicóptero do Corpo de Bombeiros encaminhou a vítima para o Hospital do Subúrbio.
articles.summary: Caso aconteceu na Avenida Afrânio Peixoto, no bairro do Lobato. Helicóptero do Corpo de Bombeiros encaminhou a vítima para o Hospital do Subúrbio.
articles.body:
Motociclista fica ferido após ter pescoço atingido por linha com cerol em Salvador — Foto: Mônica Melo/TV Bahia

Um motociclista ficou gravemente ferido após ter o pescoço cortado por uma linha de pipa com cerol, nesta segunda-feira (9), na Avenida Afrânio Peixoto, no bairro do Lobato, em Salvador .

Segundo informações apuradas pela TV Bahia no local, o corte foi profundo, mas a vítima permaneceu consciente após o acidente.

De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, uma pessoa que estava no local fez os primeiros socorros ao motociclista, utilizando uma camisa para pressionar o ferimento e conter o sangramento até a chegada do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu), que prestou atendimento ao homem.

Um helicóptero do Corpo de Bombeiros pousou na avenida e encaminhou o motociclista para o Hospital do Subúrbio.

Em entrevista à TV Bahia, uma testemunha que estava na motocicleta com a vítima contou que mora no Centro de Salvador e havia pedido ao jovem que fizesse um favor na região do Subúrbio Ferroviário.

Segundo ele, durante o trajeto, uma linha de pipa atingiu o pescoço do motociclista, que começou a gritar ao perceber o que havia acontecido. Logo depois, a vítima perdeu o controle da motocicleta e caiu na avenida.

Por causa da ocorrência, a Avenida Afrânio Peixoto ficou interditada nos dois sentidos, provocando transtornos no trânsito da região.

articles.title: 'Postcode lottery' to freeze eggs, Padiham cancer survivor says
articles.summary: A woman who survived stage four blood cancer says she no longer has access to fertility treatment.
articles.body:
A woman from Lancashire who had stage four blood cancer said she is fighting for NHS-funded fertility preservation treatment.

Mollie Mulheron, 28, said she was unable to freeze her eggs before chemotherapy because her cancer was so aggressive she needed urgent treatment.

Although she has since recovered and is cancer-free, NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria Integrated Care Board said it would not fund egg freezing because she does not meet its eligibility criteria.

Mollie said: "It's clearly unfair because the funding is there before chemotherapy, so it doesn't make sense that it's not available now."

Mollie, who lives in Padiham, was travelling in the Galapagos Islands after university when she said she started to feel ill.

After travelling back home to get checked out, doctors found a melon-sized tumour, which was "crushing my heart and left lung," Mollie said.

It took approximately 800 hours of chemotherapy, over 150 days, for Mollie to be cancer-free.

"It was hell, but I did manage to beat it," said Mollie, who runs a language academy in Lancashire.

But because the cancer was so aggressive, she said she did not have time to freeze her eggs before treatment.

Chemotherapy can affect fertility, so some cancer patients are offered fertility preservation beforehand.

Mollie said doctors at St James's Hospital in Leeds told her she could access fertility preservation after chemotherapy.

However, after moving to Padiham, she said she was told funding was not available.

"It does seem to be a postcode lottery that some places allow it and other postcodes don't at all," she said.

Mollie has started an online petition calling for better protection of young cancer survivors' fertility and to address what she says is an NHS funding gap after chemotherapy.

Mollie said her ovarian reserve had more than halved in a year and she had been told she was likely to go through an early menopause.

She fears that without fertility preservation treatment she may not be able to have children in the future.

The 28-year-old said she was struggling with the prospect of losing that option, particularly as she did not want to feel pressured into starting a family immediately after recovering from cancer.

"I'd like to have some time after having cancer just to rebuild my life," she said.

Updated National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance says healthcare professionals should discuss fertility preservation with people whose medical condition or treatment is likely to affect their fertility.

Mollie said the guidance was not mandatory and could be interpreted differently by local NHS bodies, creating inconsistencies in access to treatment.

She said the process had left her feeling frustrated and trapped in a cycle of uncertainty.

"It's just kind of going around in circles, it feels like, and it's just so unfair," she said.

A spokesperson for NHS Lancashire and South Cumbria Integrated Care Board said: "We are aware of the case and understand the patient's concerns, however, decisions such as this one are in line with the current eligibility criteria of the Assisted Conception policy for Lancashire and South Cumbria.

"Due to patient confidentiality, we are unable to comment on specific details of individual cases.

"Lancashire and South Cumbria ICB is currently working collaboratively with Greater Manchester and Cheshire and Merseyside ICBs to review a number of clinical commissioning policies, and assisted conception services have been identified as a priority, particularly in light of updated national guidance.

"The ICB would welcome any review of national policy that gives due consideration to the needs of all patients."

articles.title: Kent and Medway's first female psychiatric intensive care unit to open
articles.summary: The unit will care for women with serious mental health needs in Kent and Medway.
articles.body:
The first NHS intensive care unit for women with serious mental health needs in Kent and Medway is due to open.

Women in the region will have access to a dedicated NHS psychiatric intensive care unit for the first time, following a £4.63m investment by Kent and Medway Mental Health NHS Trust.

The 10-bed facility at Littlestone Lodge in Dartford will provide short-term, intensive care for women experiencing serious mental health difficulties who need extra support.

Dr Afifa Qazi, chief medical officer for the trust, said the opening was an important step forward and that until now women needing intensive care and support "have not been able to receive this specialist care from our team".

The unit is expected to provide around 2,500 bed days of care for women each year, and is due to welcome its first patient towards the end of November.

Qazi said: "This new service means we can now provide specialist, compassionate care at a particularly difficult time in their lives.

"Our team will take the time to get to know each woman, understand what matters to her and recognise her as a person, not just her mental health needs."

The trust said the unit would create a more joined-up pathway, helping women move smoothly between hospital wards and community services as their needs changed, with care planned around each woman's circumstances.

Two of the 10 beds will also be available to women referred by other NHS trusts, depending on individual needs.

The trust already provides intensive mental health care for men at Willow Suite, a 12-bed unit at Littlebrook Hospital. The new unit extends this specialist service to women.

People with personal experience of mental health services helped shape the unit, and its design also takes account of sensory needs, including those of women with autism and learning disabilities.

Jim Dickson, MP for Dartford, said women experiencing serious mental health difficulties deserved "care that treats them with dignity, compassion and an understanding of their individual needs".

"I'm pleased to see this new unit open in Dartford. It is an important investment in mental health services for women and their families across Kent and Medway," he said.

articles.title: 6-minute daily habit could help Ozempic users preserve muscle, expert says
articles.summary: Gary Brecka says just six minutes of daily resistance training can help protect lean body mass during Ozempic and Wegovy weight loss journeys.
articles.body: As more Americans turn to popular GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound to lose weight or manage diabetes, there is a growing focus on protecting muscle as pounds are shed. The concern comes as 11% of U.S. adults report taking these drugs for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024, according to Gallup. Lean mass, which includes muscle and other tissues, accounts for roughly a quarter to a third of the weight lost with these obesity treatments, research suggests. 4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS Gary Brecka, a biologist and longevity expert in Miami, Florida, shared with Fox News Digital his simple strategy for helping people preserve muscle — starting with just six minutes of exercise a day. "GLP-1s can be life-saving for people, especially for people who are morbidly obese or have type 2 diabetes, but they can also be fascinating shifts in someone's trajectory of their wellness journey," he said. "What's critically important for people who embark on a GLP-1 journey is to make sure that they are mitigating the lean body-mass loss." Brecka emphasized that weight loss is not exclusively fat loss. OZEMPIC USERS MAY BE MAKING A MAJOR WEIGHT-LOSS MISTAKE, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS "When most people say, ‘I want to lose weight,’ what they're really saying is, ‘I want to lose fat,’" he said. "But with GLP-1s, you have a double-edged sword. About 20% to 40% of the weight that you lose is what we call lean body mass." Lean body mass includes not only muscle, but also water, organs, blood and connective tissues, such as tendons and ligaments. Brecka emphasized that preserving lean tissue should be a priority during treatment. "You don't have to lift like a bodybuilder to mitigate lean body mass loss." Maintaining strength also helps people remain independent as they age, supporting everyday activities such as bathing, dressing and walking. "The more that we can maintain control and dominion over those, the more independent we can be," Brecka said. WEEKLY WEIGHTLIFTING SWEET SPOT MAY BE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE, STUDY FINDS Strength in minutes Challenging the body through exercise encourages it to adapt and grow stronger, Brecka said. "But when it comes to a GLP-1 journey, you've got to give up a little bit of that comfort to reach your goals," he said. Brecka recommends starting with six minutes of resistance exercise each day. "People think of weight-training or resistance training as something they've got to dedicate 60 to 90 minutes to every day, and therefore they think they don't have enough time in their day," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES It’s also important to pair the strength training with adequate protein to help preserve muscle during weight loss. Protein provides amino acids that help the body build and maintain muscle and other tissues, including tendons, ligaments and cartilage, Brecka said. ‘Snacking’ on exercise Busy people who don’t have time for lengthy gym sessions can fit resistance training into their day by "snacking" on exercise, the longevity expert said. Brecka suggested simple exercises such as holding a plank with the knees on the floor, progressing to a full plank as strength allows, or doing body-weight squats and abdominal crunches. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ He also recommended resistance exercises using dumbbells or barbells, preferably moving through a full range of motion. One example is a goblet squat, which involves holding a dumbbell near the chest while squatting and standing. "You don't have to lift like a bodybuilder to mitigate lean body mass loss," he said. "All you have to do is provide resistance for these tissues so that your body doesn't begin to reabsorb them while you're on this GLP-1 journey." In terms of frequency, Brecka said exercise should be "non-negotiable" as a daily practice. He recommends a minimum of three days of resistance training and a minimum of three days of cardiovascular training. "Cardiovascular training can be as simple as walking outside, taking your dog for a 20-minute walk," he said, adding that a weighted vest can make the same walk more challenging by increasing the load the body carries. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "If you're going to an airport, skip the moving walkway, skip the escalator, just take the steps," Brecka suggested. "There are simple things that you can do every single day … that have a dramatic impact on your body's ability to rebuild these tissues." "These small choices throughout our lifetime are what build resilience for the decades ahead." Prioritizing protein Protein does more than just support muscle, according to Brecka. Whether protein comes from chicken, beef or plant-based foods, the body breaks it down into amino acids that help build and repair muscle and other tissues, including tendons, ligaments and cartilage. "Protein is important for so many more things than just muscle and the physical things that we see on the outside," Brecka said. "It's also responsible for building these lean body mass structures." Current federal dietary guidelines recommend 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A joint advisory on GLP-1 treatment discusses the same range during active weight loss, while emphasizing that targets should be tailored to the individual. Brecka also urged patients to pay attention to declining energy or exercise performance, such as finding a previously easy flight of stairs suddenly difficult, and discuss those changes with a doctor.

articles.title: Katie Couric Televises Her Colonoscopy on TODAY in 2000 In Historic First
articles.summary: In 2000, Katie Couric got a colonoscopy, which was broadcast on TODAY.
articles.body: As TODAY marks its 75th anniversary, the TODAY Archive is revisiting legendary interviews, stories that moved us and other iconic moments from our 75 years on the air. These are the segments that shaped TODAY and created a lasting legacy. Today, we look back at when Katie Couric got a colonoscopy that aired on the show on March 7, 2000. In what may be one of the most visually striking moments ever on TODAY, Katie Couric underwent a colonoscopy in a segment that viewers watched when it aired on March 7, 2000 — a first for morning television. In the days before something could go viral, the procedure proved to be a water cooler moment, but also had a much deeper impact. “The number of colonoscopies performed ... after Ms. Couric’s campaign increased significantly. After adjusting for temporal trends, a significantly higher postcampaign colonoscopy rate was sustained for 9 months. Analysis also demonstrated a trend toward an increase in the percentage of colonoscopies performed on women” the National Institutes of Health said in 2003. “Katie Couric’s televised colon cancer awareness campaign was temporally associated with an increase in colonoscopy use in 2 different data sets,” the agency added. The TODAY co-anchor wanted to raise awareness about colon cancer following the death of her husband, Jay Monahan, from the disease in 1998. How Did Katie Couric Prep for Her Colonoscopy? The segment, which Couric celebrated on TODAY in 2025, began with her drinking multiple glasses of NuLytely, a solution used to clean the colon before a colonoscopy. She sucked on some limes to help make it more palatable. “I’m not sure I’d order it at a restaurant,” she said. What Happened During the Colonoscopy? The clip then moved on to the next day, when Couric went to a hospital and met with her doctor, Dr. Ford, and his team, which prepped her for the procedure. The doctors and nurses enjoyed a few laughs with Couric, who joked about not being held accountable for her behavior while being sedated. He gave her some Demerol, which he promised would make her groggy. “It’s a nice, relaxing feeling,” he said while he also assuaged her concerns when she said she’s feeling nervous. Couric said she was starting to feel tired, while Dr. Ford expressed his confidence the medicine is working because she was having trouble talking. “I have a pretty little colon,” she said later while viewers saw a monitor of what was presumably that body part while they performed the exam, much to her surprise. “Yeah, we’re doing it,” Dr. Ford said. “We’re almost done.” He said her blood vessels were healthy and normal. Couric, placed on her side while the doctor stood behind her, then asked what was at the bottom of the screen. “It’s just like when you’re driving through a tunnel and your headlights haven’t reached the spot, it looks dark, but once your headlights get up to it, you realize that it’s clear,” he said. A nurse then moved Couric onto her back before Ford showed her where her small intestine was. “In other words, we’re six feet up,” he said. “That’s reassuring, Dr. Ford. Thank you for sharing that point with me,” she said, while getting him to confirm that colons are generally six feet long, no matter how tall the person is. “We’ve reached the end of the colon,” she said. Dr. Ford then got another “definitive” look at the colon. The Examination Came to a Successful End “It’s as clean as a whistle. This is a perfectly normal examination, up to this point,” the doctor said shortly before they wrapped up. Ford also said he kept her sedated enough so she wasn’t “terrified,” adding, “But you didn’t need any more, so you could interact.” As for how Couric was feeling post-examination, she said, “The only discomfort was really, sort of, when you blew air in me, I guess ... But, other than that, I didn’t feel a thing.” The segment ended with Couric showing a colonoscope, the tool which Ford used on her to perform the procedure. She showed how it moved up and down, side to side, and how it was equipped with a brush to take out a polyp and get cells from the colon for pathology to determine if the polyp is cancerous or not. She concluded by reminding viewers of the importance of early detection.

articles.title: Senior doctors at Glasgow hospital in care delay warning
articles.summary: Consultants at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital say conditions for emergency patients there are deteriorating.
articles.body:
Senior emergency doctors at Scotland's biggest hospital have written to the healthcare watchdog warning of harm to patients from delays to care.

The consultants also warned of uncontrollable system failure, in a letter sent to Healthcare Improvement Scotland (His) in July.

They said the situation in the emergency department at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital (QEUH) in Glasgow had deteriorated since their last review, which was undertaken in 2024 and published a year later.

That report found that poor relationships between managers and consultants was likely to have had a detrimental impact on patient care.

The July letter said staff were being forced to step down patients from resuscitation areas and move people into corridors to address "sustained overcapacity".

They added that there was no effective strategy to address the problems, and said evidence now clearly linked overcrowding in accident and emergency areas to higher death rates.

Emergency doctor 'completely terrified' of looming winter pressures on NHS

Expert calls for safety review at Scotland's troubled superhospital

A spokesperson for Health Improvement Scotland said it continued to "take the concerns raised by staff in the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital Emergency Department seriously".

The statement added: "As part of our ongoing follow-up work, we will be meeting frontline staff and reviewing progress against the recommendations from our previous review during November. We have also made Scottish government colleagues aware of the ongoing concerns and pressures that have been raised with us.

"It is for NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde to implement the changes required and to address the issues identified. We expect the board to demonstrate progress in implementing the recommendations and responding to the concerns raised by staff.

"Given our ongoing review activity, it would not be appropriate to comment in detail on specific correspondence or to pre-empt our further findings from our follow up work."

The Scottish Liberal Democrats called on ministers to act on the letter.

Their health spokesman, Adam Harley MSP, said: "This letter is chilling. The Scottish government needs to wake up to the crisis at the QEUH and intervene.

"We cannot accept this constant crisis as the status quo.

"That patients who need resuscitation at one of our busiest hospitals cannot take their safety for granted shows an utter failure of accountability, and proves that our NHS is in dire need of rescue."

NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde (NHSGGC) said they continued to address the issues raised in the letter.

A statement said a programme of improvement work was ongoing to deal with patient flow and numbers.

It said: "NHSGGC recognises that, despite the work to date, further support is required in the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital. In recognising this, the continuation of our improvement work, including a refreshed whole system approach, is a priority .

"We recognise that some patients continue to wait too long within the emergency department, particularly when there are pressures on hospital capacity and delays in discharging patients who are clinically ready to leave, and improving this situation for both our patients and colleagues is really important to us."

The board said the department continued to be under pressure and patient safety remained their highest priority.

Health Secretary Angela Constance said she was aware of the concerns raised by A&E staff at the QEUH, and agreed current waiting times were not acceptable.

"We do know that emergency departments across Scotland continue to experience that sustained pressure," she said.

She stressed that it was important for people to access a "full range" of other services - like GPs and pharmacies where appropriate - instead of going straight to A&E.

Constance said she would be engaging with both NHSGGC and HIS on the specifics raised in the letter.

She said she would "seek assurance and scrutiny" from HIS, adding: "It is the role of Healthcare Improvement Scotland to ensure that local managers and decisions at board level can demonstrate that grip and control of emerging situations".

articles.title: A Dietitian’s No. 1 Protein-Packed Ingredient to Boost Bone Health
articles.summary: When bone health is your top food priority, look for protein and calcium, a dietitian says. This one staple food provides both to support your bone density.
articles.body: When bone health is your top priority, you’ll want to look for foods with specific nutrients. That includes protein, calcium and vitamin D, says Natalie Rizzo, registered dietitian and TODAY nutrition editor. These nutrients work together, she adds. That’s why one of her favorite foods to support bone health is packed with both plant-based protein and calcium. Expert Tip of the Day: Try This Plant Protein for Bone Health “Tofu is probably the most beneficial for bone health in terms of plant-based proteins because it’s actually made with calcium,” Rizzo said previously. “The way that a block of tofu is coagulated is with calcium sulfate,” she explained. And the firmer the tofu, the more calcium you’re likely to get. Why It Matters Calcium is one of the main building blocks of bone, and getting enough of it as we age is a simple yet effective way to support bone density. On top of that, calcium supports the health of your teeth, skin, nails and hair. Your body’s muscle functions, nerve transmissions and hormone secretion also rely on calcium, dietitians explained to TODAY.com previously. And, of course, we also need protein for healthy bones. And plant proteins, like tofu, come with additional nutrients that aren’t often found in animal products. In this case, tofu provides anti-inflammatory compounds called isoflavones, Rizzo says, and it contains phytoestrogens, which may help alleviate some symptoms of menopause. All of this makes tofu a great option to support your bone health, especially in midlife. How to Get Started If you’ve never tried making tofu before, it can be a little daunting. Make sure you select the right kind of tofu for the dish you want to whip up. Keep in mind that firm and extra-firm tofu tends to have the most protein and calcium per serving, but you will likely need to drain it of excess moisture before cooking. Here are a few easy ways to start incorporating this plant-based protein into your meals: Air-Fryer Salt and Pepper TofuChipotle Pineapple Tofu SkewersSpicy and Crunchy Garlic Tofu Miso Asparagus Sheet Pan-Tofu You can also blend tofu into smoothies and dips to add protein and nutrients without affecting the flavor. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Men and women who smoke marijuana may experience different effects, study suggests
articles.summary: UCLA researchers found occasional male cannabis users reported stronger effects like anxiety and elevated heart rate than women with similar THC levels.
articles.body: Men who use cannabis occasionally may feel stronger effects from the drug than women with similar use habits, new research suggests. The UCLA Health study, published in the journal Neuropsychopharmacology, included 44 healthy adults between the ages of 21 and 55, evenly split between men and women. Researchers divided participants based on whether they used cannabis frequently or occasionally. Each participant took part in three separate sessions: smoking cannabis with no THC, a lower amount of THC or a higher amount. They did not know which one they were receiving at the time. MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS Among those who used cannabis occasionally, men reported feeling more high, sedated and impaired than women with similar use habits, according to the study. The men also reported more unpleasant effects, including anxiety, and their heart rate rose significantly after using active cannabis. Blood THC levels alone did not appear to explain the difference. Men and women who used cannabis occasionally had similar peak THC levels, even though the men reported stronger effects, researchers found. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The pattern was different among people who used cannabis more often. Men and women in the frequent-use group generally responded similarly to active cannabis. Frequent users were also more likely than occasional users to say they liked the effects, wanted to use cannabis again and chose to take more during the study, regardless of gender. The findings challenge some previous research suggesting women may be more sensitive to the effects of cannabis. "Much of what we thought we knew about sex differences in cannabis effects came from animal research and from human studies that pooled data from different trials," Dr. Ziva Cooper, the study's principal investigator and director of the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids, said in a press release. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "When we designed a study to look at sex and frequency of use at the same time, and controlled for hormones, the picture changed," she added. The researchers controlled for menstrual cycle timing among the women in the study, who were not using hormonal birth control. The findings suggest that a person's cannabis habits may be important when considering how men and women respond to the drug. "Sex and cannabis use history can both shape how someone experiences the effects of cannabis," lead author Dr. Stephanie Lake, a researcher at the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids, said in the release. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Studying both together is key to understanding who is most at risk of higher-risk, unpleasant or beneficial experiences from cannabis." There were several limitations to the findings, the researchers acknowledged. The study was small, with just 44 participants, and several of the findings involving occasional male users came from exploratory analyses, meaning they need to be confirmed in larger studies. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The cannabis used in the experiment contained 4% or 10% THC, which researchers noted is weaker than many cannabis products sold today, where THC levels are commonly 20% or higher. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Researchers said larger studies are needed to better understand whether men and women develop tolerance to cannabis differently and how those differences could affect the risk of cannabis use disorder. Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

articles.title: California police probe 'suspicious circumstances' after nearly 20 hospitalized following half-marathon
articles.summary: Santa Barbara Police Department is probing suspicious circumstances after 19 half-marathon runners sought emergency care for unusual symptoms.
articles.body: Police in California are investigating "suspicious circumstances" after nearly 20 people were hospitalized following a half-marathon, with several runners reporting "unusual symptoms." Santa Barbara Cottage Hospital alerted police after several runners from Sunday's half-marathon came in "seeking medical treatment for unusual symptoms" following the race, the Santa Barbara Police Department said in a news release, according to CBS Los Angeles. "The cause of the reported symptoms has not been confirmed," police said. "There is no specific action recommended for the public at this time; however, participants who feel unwell should seek medical attention and follow guidance from healthcare professionals." GRAND CANYON MYSTERY ILLNESS REPORTEDLY TRIGGERS NPS INVESTIGATION AFTER RAFTERS REPORT ALARMING SYMPTOMS Police said those hospitalized either arrived on their own or were transported by ambulance. A spokesperson for Cottage Health said in a statement to the outlet that the number of emergency visits from the half-marathon was larger than expected. SEND US A TIP "We have a larger than expected number of emergency visits that are tracked to participants of this morning's organized run in SB," Cottage Health said. "This morning 19 patients arrived at Cottage EDs, a number of them with similar symptoms of undetermined cause." The hospital spokesperson said they are still trying to determine if the symptoms were caused by heat or other factors. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST A spokesperson for the group who organized the half-marathon said they believe the hospitalizations were heat-related, according to ABC 7. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "At this time, we have no reason to believe that there was anything out of the ordinary that occurred during today's race, besides typical heat-related illness or exhaustion that can take place while participating in long endurance events such as a half marathon," the spokesperson said. articles.title: The 1 Thing This Doctor Would Never Use as a Sleep Aid — Even Though It Works
articles.summary: A sleep specialist explains why turning to alcohol for sleep will do you more harm than good. While it helps you fall asleep, the longterm effects are dangerous.
articles.body: TODAY’s Never Have I Ever series offers guidance about procedures and practices our trusted health experts would never participate in. Discover why they should be avoided and which healthy practices you should turn to instead. If you rely on alcohol to help you sleep, you’re onto something. “Alcohol does help people fall asleep quicker,” Dr. Saema Tahir, board-certified physician specializing in sleep disorders, pulmonary disease and critical care medicine, tells TODAY.com. When alcohol binds to the neurotransmitters responsible for creating a calming or sedating effect in the brain, it helps you drift off. Unfortunately, that’s where the benefits end. That nighttime glass (or glasses) of wine won’t help you stay asleep or feel rested the next morning, Tahir explains. So if you develop a long-term reliance on alcohol at bedtime, you’ll likely find that it’s done you more harm than good. Never Have I Ever: Used Alcohol as a Sleep Aid Alcohol “tricks you” into thinking it’s a sleep aid, says Tahir, because it reduces the amount of time you waste tossing and turning before falling asleep. But, “as the alcohol metabolizes throughout the night, it breaks down the type of sleep you have later on,” she says. Once you’re asleep, the body goes through various cycles and stages of REM sleep — the rapid eye movement that happens when you dream — and non-REM sleep. Both are essential for restorative rest. Alcohol disrupts REM sleep, says Tahir. Even if you were technically asleep all night long, it won’t have been the kind of sleep you needed to function at your best, instead leaving you feeling groggy, irritable and depressed. What to Do Instead If you haven’t used alcohol to help you get some shuteye, says Tahir, don’t start. Instead, Tahir recommends cutting off your alcohol intake three to four hours before bedtime. And for an even more restful night’s sleep, make sure you have a consistent sleep schedule, where you sleep and wake at the same times daily, and sleep in a cool, totally dark room. If you rely on alcohol before bed and find that it works for you, it’s likely because you’ve already tried all the other tried-and-true sleep hygiene advice that’s out there, says Tahir, like taking warm showers before bed and avoiding screens. But these habits may not be working for you because you may have a sleep disorder that requires professional assistance, says Tahir. Also, relying on alcohol to help you fall asleep could be a sign of alcohol use disorder, she adds. In either case, consulting a medical professional is critical. Weaning off a reliance on alcohol is an involved process that requires supervision, says Tahir. For example, it may involve medications to prevent the sometimes-deadly effects of withdrawal. And sleep disorders also should be treated by a specialist — your primary care doctor can help refer you, Tahir says. Once you see one, you may encounter one of the following diagnoses: Insomnia, whether it keeps you from falling asleep, staying asleep or waking up earlier than intendedSleep apnea, a breathing-related sleep disorderRestless leg syndrome, a movement conditionCircadian rhythm disorder, which disrupts your body’s natural sleep and wake cycles Alcohol tends to impact sleep apnea, insomnia and periodic limb movement disorders most. But even those with sleep disorders including hypersomnia or narcolepsy, says Tahir, will find that alcohol exacerbates the degree of sleepiness they’ll feel throughout the day. The next step is treatment, which can mean medication, sleep devices or treating another issue that’s causing the sleep disorder. No matter what, “alcohol is never a solution,” says Tahir.

articles.title: NBC’s Chloe Melas Shares 1st Symptoms of Bowel Disease She Almost Ignored
articles.summary: In her early 20s, NBC’s Chloe Melas was navigating New York City as a busy young journalist. But she developed digestive issues that turned out to be serious.
articles.body: In her early 20s, NBC’s Chloe Melas was trying to make her way in New York City as a busy young journalist. But she was plagued with digestive issues. “I started noticing that I needed to go to the bathroom a lot. And when I say a lot, (I mean) sometimes 15 to 20 times a day,” Melas, an entertainment correspondent, recalled during a Nov. 9 segment on the TODAY Show. Sometimes, Melas says, she would also find some blood in her stool. “And at first, I ignored it,” she added. It wasn’t until her mom urged her to see a gastroenterologist that she started to take her symptoms more seriously. After a colonoscopy, Melas was diagnosed in 2012 with ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Her new book, “The Girl’s Guide to Guts: Everything Your Doc Didn’t Tell You (But Your Bestie Would),” chronicles her experience with IBD and offers tips to navigate life with a digestive condition. What Is Inflammatory Bowel Disease? Melas was first diagnosed with proctitis, a condition involving inflammation of the rectum. Her doctor prescribed medication, she told TODAY.com previously, but she began feeling backed up and unable to defecate. And she was still seeing blood in her stool. After two years of these symptoms, her doctor ordered a colonoscopy, which revealed an underlying disease: ulcerative colitis, a condition that causes inflammation and sores in the colon, according to the Mayo Clinic. Ulcerative colitis is one of the two most common forms of IBD, the other being Crohn’s disease, Dr. Natalie Azar, NBC medical contributor, said on the TODAY Show. These conditions are auto-inflammatory diseases, she explained, meaning they arise when the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy cells. IBD is distinct from another similar-sounding issue, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), which is instead thought to be caused by a problem with the body’s gut-brain connection, Azar added. People with IBD may also have symptoms that show up in the eyes, joints and skin, Azar noted, and they’re at a higher risk for colon cancer. Digestive Symptoms to Never Ignore Part of why Melas is so open about her IBD experience is because she knows other people, particularly women, may not get the care they need without this type of knowledge. Some symptoms of IBD and IBS can also be signs of issues including diverticulitis (an inflammation of the walls of the large intestine) and even colon cancer, Azar noted. “So many women that I have talked to over the years, they might have had some blood in the stool be dismissed by a doctor as a hemorrhoid, and it turns out to be colon cancer. And these are women in their 30s,” Melas said. “That’s why we wanted to put all this information in one (book),” she explained, “so that people feel less alone and laugh a little, but also get the information that they need.” Azar said it’s important not to ignore symptoms such as: Blood in the stoolUrgency to go to the bathroomAnemiaLow-grade feverUnintentional weight loss It may be uncomfortable to talk about bathroom issues like these, but, “If you have those things, please go to a doctor,” Melas said. “Do not ignore them.”

articles.title: FDA orders new warning on GLP-1s over rare eye condition linked to sudden blindness
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness.
articles.body: The Food and Drug Administration said Monday that GLP-1 drugmakers must add a warning label about a rare eye condition that can cause sudden blindness. The condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, affects the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. When blood flow to the nerve is reduced or blocked, it can cause sudden vision loss. The condition is permanent with no known treatment. The FDA said “there is a potential increased risk of rare NAION” in people taking GLP-1 drugs. The agency’s requirement applies to all GLP-1s, including Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Wegovy and Eli Lilly’s Mounjaro and Zepbound, as well as several older GLP-1 diabetes medications. Spokespeople for both Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly said patient safety is their top priority. Previous research has found that GLP-1 use may increase the risk of NAION, and Lilly has said it was aware of studies on the potential link. The FDA said it began looking into a possible link after a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology that found diabetes patients prescribed semaglutide were four times as likely to develop NAION as those not prescribed the drug. The agency said it reviewed reports of side effects submitted to its adverse event monitoring system and analyzed data from multiple clinical trials. Cases of NAION have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 drugs, the FDA found. However, FDA scientists were not able to identify a mechanism for how the drugs could increase the risk of the eye condition. Risk factors for NAION can overlap with conditions seen in people taking GLP-1 drugs, including Type 2 diabetes, obesity, sleep apnea and hypertension. Dr. Manjot Gill, an ophthalmologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, said the FDA’s mandate for a warning label was appropriate. While it remains unclear whether the drugs cause the eye condition, she said, it’s been well-documented that they may increase the risk. Even so, there is little cause for immediate anxiety, Gill said, noting that the condition is extremely rare. “We don’t want patients to really get overly concerned and anxious and to stop these medications,” Gill said. “It’s fine to issue this warning more so for public awareness so that patients, should they experience any kind of change in vision, that they do actually go and seek the care of an eye provider.” NAION is the second most common optic nerve disease in the U.S., occurring in up to 10 out of 100,000 people over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. “Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss,” with GLP-1 use, the FDA said in the release. The drug labels from Novo Nordisk and Lilly also carry other warnings, including for pancreatitis, gallbladder problems and kidney injury. The labels also carry a black box warning — the FDA’s strongest safety warning — about a possible risk of thyroid tumors.

articles.title: ¿Qué enfermedad tiene el papá de Shakira y cuál es su estado de salud actual?
articles.standfirst: “Una semana difícil”: Shakira rompe el silencio y esto es lo que se sabe sobre la salud de su papá
articles.summary: “Una semana difícil”: Shakira rompe el silencio y esto es lo que se sabe sobre la salud de su papá
articles.body: La salud de William Mebarak Chadid, padre de la superestrella colombiana Shakira, ha vuelto a acaparar la atención mediática y la preocupación de sus seguidores tras una serie de altibajos médicos que encendieron las alarmas en los últimos días. La propia artista rompió el silencio a través de sus redes sociales para agradecer el apoyo recibido, en medio de una ola de especulaciones sobre el estado actual de su padre, quien está próximos a cumplir los 96 años de edad. A inicios de noviembre, el programa Al Rojo Vivo, de Telemundo, reportó que Mebarak, de 95 años, habría ingresado de urgencia a una clínica de Barranquilla. La información no incluía causas ni diagnóstico, pero encendió la alarma entre seguidores de la cantante y motivó especulaciones sobre un deterioro repentino de su salud. Shakira viajó a Barranquilla y fue vista el 6 de noviembre acompañando a su padre durante un recorrido por el norte de la ciudad. En las imágenes difundidas por medios locales, Mebarak aparece movilizándose en silla de ruedas y con apoyo de personal asistencial, mientras la artista camina a su lado. No hay, hasta ahora, una 'enfermedad actual' confirmada públicamente. Lo que sí está documentado es una secuencia de problemas de salud desde 2022, que han llevado a Mebarak a requerir atención hospitalaria en varias ocasiones. La combinación de tres factores alimentó la preocupación: la edad de Mebarak, sus antecedentes médicos serios y la aparición de Shakira en Barranquilla en plena semana. Además, las imágenes de su padre en silla de ruedas y con acompañamiento médico fueron interpretadas por algunos como señal de una nueva crisis, aunque no constituyen evidencia de una hospitalización. Fuentes cercanas a la familia desmintieron la internación y señalaron que Mebarak permanecía en su residencia, acompañado por sus seres queridos y bajo sus tratamientos habituales. Esa versión fue recogida por medios colombianos como El Tiempo, El Colombiano y La FM. El estado de salud del padre de Shakira ha estado bajo estrecha vigilancia médica desde hace varios años, acumulando diversas complicaciones propias de su avanzada edad: Ante la incertidumbre generada por los recientes reportes de prensa sobre una "difícil semana" a nivel familiar, Shakira utilizó su cuenta oficial para enviar un mensaje de gratitud a quienes han estado pendientes de su padre: “Gracias a todos por sus mensajes de cariño en esta difícil semana. Mi familia y yo nos encontramos profundamente agradecidos”, expresó la intérprete de Waka Waka y Hips Don't Lie. Por su parte, ni la artista ni su círculo cercano han emitido comunicados médicos oficiales detallando una nueva internación hospitalaria reciente, manteniendo el hermetismo que suelen manejar respecto a la privacidad de su núcleo familiar. Para los fanáticos de Shakira, William Mebarak no es solo un padre, sino su máxima inspiración, su confidente y el motor de muchas de sus canciones y etapas artísticas. Cada vez que el ex periodista y escritor enfrenta quebrantos de salud, las alertas se activan de inmediato en el mundo del entretenimiento internacional, convirtiendo su evolución médica en uno de los temas más buscados en buscadores y redes sociales.

articles.title: Julianne Moore Shares Her 3 Non-Negotiable Habits for Healthy Aging
articles.summary: Julianne Moore takes extra care when it comes to looking after her body and her brain. In an interview with TODAY.com, she reveals the practices that help most.
articles.body: Julianne Moore, 65, knows that healthy aging is all about how you feel, not how you look. The Oscar-winning actor, who stars in the upcoming movie, “The Debut,” reveals exactly how she looks after her physical and mental health as she gets older. “I think the most important thing is function, isn’t it? That’s what it’s really about. I think we put a lot of emphasis on how we look, but really what we should care about is how well we function,” Moore tells TODAY.com in an exclusive interview. “It’s what our energy levels are like, what our strength levels are like,” the actor adds. “You want to be able to do all the things that you like doing and do them as efficiently as possible,” says Moore, who recently partnered with Lilly on their “Brain Health Matters” campaign. “It really is to encourage people to take their brain health as seriously as they take any other kind of health,” says Moore. The actor hopes to inspire people to ask about cognitive assessments at their regular checkups, especially if they are experiencing memory or thinking issues. Neurodegenerative decline is a topic Moore knows well. In 2014, she won the Academy Award for best actress for her performance in “Still Alice,” which is about a university linguistics professor diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer’s disease. In her own life, Moore takes regular steps to protect her body and brain as she ages because she has no intention of slowing down anytime soon. It’s allowed her to take part in the upcoming film, adding to her decorated filmography, and in some other big moments that have happened this year, including her son’s wedding this October. Here are Moore’s non-negotiable health habits she practices to prioritize her brain health and physical wellbeing: Strength Training Moore’s approach to exercise has changed dramatically as she gets older, especially in recent years. “You don’t think about it when you’re younger, in terms of exercising, but now, maintaining muscle mass is really important,” says Moore. “I think strength training has been a big, big new development for me,” she adds. Most people reach peak muscle mass around the age of 30, after which point it declines gradually with age. Menopause can accelerate the loss of muscle and bone density, which is why it’s strength training is crucial for women over the age of 50, TODAY.com reported previously. Learning New Skills One of the most important habits Moore has adopted to protect her brain health as she ages is learning new skills and hobbies. At 65, she’s attempting to master a new language. She tries to practice every day, despite the challenges. “I’m trying to learn French, not successfully,” she says. The actor also speaks some German, which she flexed during her acceptance speech for an award at the Zurich Film Festival. “Honestly, I think it’s something that’s important in terms of your quality of life, just to keep kind of engaged and interested,” says Moore. “The more new things you learn, the more interested I think you are in your life,” Moore adds. In addition to learning a new language, Moore has taken up ceramics, which she works on regularly. Yoga Daily movement is another non-negotiable health habit for Moore. “One of the things that I do in my daily life to prioritize my health is, I do a lot of yoga,” she says. Yoga is an accessible form of exercise which promotes both physical and mental wellbeing. Practicing yoga regularly can help improve flexibility, build strength and tone the muscles. The practice can also reduce stress and anxiety — which can take a real toll on the brain. Moore incorporates Ashtanga yoga into her routine. During the pandemic, she kept consistent by taking virtual yoga classes, she revealed in an Instagram post. As part of her partnership with the “Brain Health Matters” campaign, Moore encourages others to prioritize their brain health and get regular screenings. “The brain is the control center of the body. It’s going to determine how you function,” says Moore.

articles.title: Merger speculations script confusion within NCP, MLAs seek clarity from top leadership
articles.summary: NCP merger rumours spark confusion in Sunetra Pawar-led faction; MLAs seek clarity as Praful Patel, Parth Pawar meet Sharad Pawar amid mixed signals.
articles.body: PUNE: Speculations over a disgruntled section of NCP’s attempt to revive merger talks with the rival faction has triggered confusion within the Sunetra Pawar-led party, prompting several party members, including a few MLAs, allegedly “in the dark” to seek clarity from the top leadership on the issue.Amid the differences within the NCP’s top leadership, party chief Sunetra addressed over 30 lawmakers last week. According to those who attended the meeting, there was no discussion on the proposed merger.“While some senior party leaders privately admit that attempts are being made to explore various options, including the possibility of a merger, there has been no direct communication from the party leadership on the issue,” an NCP MLA from Pune district told TOI.Speculations gained momentum after NCP working president Praful Patel last week met NCP (SP) chief Sharad Pawar, then admitted to Mumbai’s Breach Candy Hospital. Following the meeting, Patel said he would meet Pawar again after Nov 10, when political discussions could take place. Subsequently, Sunetra’s elder son and Rajya Sabha member Parth Pawar met his granduncle Sharad Pawar twice in two days in Mumbai.“With confusion growing within the party, we want our senior leaders to convene another meeting of all MLAs and address our concerns. We expect a meeting between the MLAs and the core committee members to be held in Mumbai after the Diwali festival,” another MLA said.Even before the meeting between Pawar and Patel, a section of NCP members sought greater clarity from their party seniors on the merger issue.Merger talks had come to a halt following the death of former deputy chief minister Ajit Pawar in a plane crash on Jan 28. State NCP president Sunil Tatkare had then said no merger discussions were taking place between the two factions. He changed his stance a few days ago and said he was aware of the parleys and the merger would have taken place by now had Ajit Pawar been alive.Reacting to Tatkare’s statement, NCP national spokesperson Umesh Patil said the state party president’s remarks were contradictory. “There has been a complete shift in his (Tatkare’s) earlier stand on the merger issue. As he is the state president of our party, we cannot seek an explanation from him. The media should ask him what prompted him to change his stance,” Patil said.Speaking about the merger proposal, Patil said it was easier said than done. He claimed that implementing such a move would upset several party members, from the top leadership to the grassroots level.“At present, these are two separate parties, each with its own organisational structure across every district. If we hypothetically assume that a merger takes place, several office-bearers, from the block- and tehsil-level to the district-level, would have to step down to accommodate their counterparts from the other faction. This would upset several members on both sides,” Patil said.NCP (SP) has maintained that there had been no discussions on a merger within its party. The party’s MLA and Sharad Pawar’s grandnephew Rohit Pawar met the NCP (SP) chief in Mumbai on Monday.“I visited him to seek his blessings on the occasion of Diwali and to enquire about his health. articles.title: Gordon Ramsay Shows Off Toned Core in IG Post. The 3 Health Habits That Got Him Here
articles.summary: Gordon Ramsay posted a shirtless photo on Instagram in celebration of his 60th birthday. Discover the fitness routine that helped build those abs.
articles.body: Gordon Ramsay is looking fitter than ever as he enters his 60s. The British celebrity chef turned up the heat when he shared a shirtless Instagram photo of himself on Nov. 9 in honor of his 60th birthday the day before. Ramsay posed in the black-and-white photo wearing a bodysuit pulled down to his hips. “Thank you everyone for the incredible birthday messages!” he captioned the image. “Day 2 of being 60……LFG !!!!” he wrote in the caption. Ramsay’s “Next Level Baker” co-star Carla Hall cheered him on in the comments of his post, writing, “You betta WERK SEXTY” alongside a fire emoji. Fans also congratulated Ramsay on his toned physique. “JUST BECAUSE HE’S NOT IN THE KITCHEN DOESN’T MEAN HE AIN’T COOKING,” wrote one. “Chef looking leaner and cleaner than a medium rare Wellington let’s goooo!” added another. The dad of six is known to be as passionate about fitness as he is about food, even competing in marathons and triathlons. Ramsay also tailors his daily eating habits to focus on nutrients as well as taste. Ahead, his three healthy lifestyle habits: Swimming, Strength Training and More Ramsay’s passion for sports and exercise began when he was young. As a teen, he played soccer in a county-wide league, but after being sidelined by a knee injury at 18, he began focusing on cooking. After turning 40, frustrated by the pounds he’d put on over the years, Ramsay decided to get active again, Men’s Health U.K, reported. In 2013, he competed in the Ironman World Championships and has gone on to participate in triathlons, marathons and half-marathons, too. To stay in shape, Ramsay begins most weekdays with a short run and also devotes time to working on his core strength. If time allows in the evenings, he’ll pull out his exercise bike. “Anywhere I go, whether it’s a swim, a bike ride, or even a walk — keeping fit is essential. A healthy lifestyle leads a healthy life. And the energy you get from even a 20-minute training session, not necessarily every day but every other day, adding just 1% to that, gets you to where you want to go,” Ramsay told Men’s Health U.K. in 2024. Ramsay’s favorite quick and easy exercise? Pushups. He drops to the floor to do 25 pushups every morning, he told the outlet. On weekends, Ramsay takes things up a notch by doing long swim sessions and intense 60-minute strength workouts. Focusing on Protein Though he’s known for his culinary creativity on television, the celebrity chef’s daily diet is all about packing in nutrients. In August, Ramsay told Men’s Health U.K. he begins each day with a protein shake. Lunch is scrambled eggs and dinner is chicken or fish, preferably poached and not boiled. “Boiling it is going to give it a texture like f------ Gandhi’s flip-flop,’ he told the publication. Eating smaller meals throughout the day also helps to keep his energy up. “You’re lethargic after you’ve eaten, right? You’ve got to stay on your toes. It’s like a ballerina — tiny little mouthfuls, tiny little tastings,’ Ramsay explained. Achieving New Goals Anyone who’s watched Ramsey in the kitchen knows he demands as much of himself as he does his contestants. So perhaps it’s no surprise he continues raising the bar for himself when it comes to fitness. In September, Ramsay told Business Traveler that he has a special goal in mind for the 2027 London Marathon — to finish the race in under three and a half hours. “I want to run a marathon faster in my 60s than I did in my 30s,” Ramsay said, “just to prove that you can do that kind of stuff.”

articles.title: New California law will restrict sales of some muscle-building supplements to minors
articles.summary: Gavin Newsom signed AB 2030 restricting diet pills and muscle building supplements for minors, but questions remain about creatine and protein products.
articles.body: Gavin Newsom has signed legislation banning the sale of some "muscle-building supplements" to Californians under 18 years of age. The legislation (AB 2030), which was signed on Sept. 28, covers over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building. It will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027. "Nonprescribed, medically unapproved products may cause dangerous side effects," the governor’s office said in its announcement. "Products can be mislabeled or contaminated with substances such as steroids." WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD California’s law restricts minors’ access to supplements marketed for muscle building – specifically, those that are "labeled, marketed or otherwise represented for the purpose of achieving weight loss or building muscle." Courts may consider whether a product contains "creatine, green tea extract, raspberry ketone, garcinia cambogia or green coffee bean extract," the legislation states. The law does not impose an outright ban on all creatine products. Restrictions depend on how the supplements are labeled, advertised and marketed to consumers. TAKING DAILY SUPPLEMENT MAY HELP PRESERVE MUSCLE AS YOU AGE — EVEN WITHOUT EXERCISE The law does not apply to people under 18 who have a prescription for an over-the-counter diet pill or dietary supplement for weight loss or muscle-building. The release cites research indicating that nearly one in 10 adolescents have used such products. It also references studies linking over-the-counter diet pill use to a sixfold greater likelihood of an eating disorder diagnosis within three years. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES The announcement does not specify whether whey protein or creatine products are included in the ban. Sellers who do not adhere to the new law will face civil fines of up to $500 per violation. "Nonprescribed, medically unapproved products may cause dangerous side effects." The American Herbal Products Association, based in Maryland, released a statement opposing the law. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Lacking any scientific justification, AB 2030 casts a shadow over safe, beneficial products," said Robert Marriott, the association's vice president of regulatory and government affairs, in the statement. The organization argues that the law's scope is unclear and notes that it does not explicitly exempt protein products. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The Center for Science in the Public Interest, based in Washington, D.C., shared public support of the new legislation. POPULAR DRINKS LINKED TO HEART ATTACKS, CARDIAC ARREST IN YOUNG ADULTS, STUDY FINDS "Manufacturers of these products often prey on kids and teens with deceptive claims that lack any scientific evidence," said Jensen Jose, a regulatory counsel at CSPI, which co-sponsored the legislation. Dr. Sigrid Wolf, a pediatric sports medicine physician at Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago, recently addressed the use of creatine products among teenagers, stating that evidence of benefits is limited. POISON CENTERS LINK GROWING BENADRYL ABUSE AMONG TEENS TO DANGEROUS SOCIAL MEDIA TRENDS "In some cases, they might even be dangerous," wrote Wolf, who is a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' sports medicine committee, in an article published on HealthyChildren.org, the American Academy of Pediatrics' parenting website. "Creatine can come with negative side effects such as weight gain, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Studies show that many supplements contain harmful substances that go undetected," she added, instead recommending prioritizing nutrition, training, sleep and hydration. Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

articles.title: Llanrwst man 'nearly died' after toothache led to sepsis and heart condition
articles.summary: Doctors told Danny Ellis it was a "miracle" he was alive after his first heart surgery failed.
articles.body:
What seemed like a simple case of toothache led to a rare heart condition, sepsis and doctors believing Danny Ellis had just a 1% chance of survival.

The 42-year-old from Llanrwst in Conwy county began experiencing tooth pain in April, and went to the dentist where he was given antibiotics.

But the pain kept returning and it was not until he was left with red marks on his body that he was finally rushed to hospital.

Doctors told him it was a "miracle" he was still alive after an initial heart operation failed, and he suffered a series of strokes - but he pulled through against the odds.

The recovery process will continue for at least another 12 months, Danny said, and he will likely be on medication for the rest of his life, but little milestones are getting him through.

"At the moment, I'm able to take my daughter to school, and that's enough for now," he said.

"I still feel different on my left side, and I can easily get tired and forget what I'm supposed to say at times, but I hope that will improve with time."

Danny said after the toothache got worse, an X-ray at his dentist in Colwyn Bay showed no signs of infection, and he returned home with another course of antibiotics.

A pattern which saw the pain ease and return continued for several weeks and Danny noticed he was losing his strength and red marks were appearing on his body.

"The pain was terrible and I had to take a week off work, something I would never do," said Danny, who runs the Spar shop in Betws-y-Coed, as well as Gwalia bakery in Pwllheli, Gwynedd.

"The symptoms were starting to get worse, and the pain too, especially in my legs. I didn't know what was going on."

By Father's Day on 21 June, Danny was feeling "out of it" and was "unable to remember what I'd received as presents".

When his wife Ceri arrived home from work, she found him lying on the couch with bruises on his body.

They went to the GP surgery in Betws-y-Coed on 23 June and, after several tests, Danny was rushed by ambulance to Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor.

"I remember seeing the nurse run out of the room to call for an ambulance," Danny said.

When he told doctors at the hospital that he had a toothache and had been on antibiotics, their "face immediately changed" and they ordered an echocardiogram , which scans the heart.

The scan found a hole in the mitral valve in Danny's heart, and it was also discovered he had developed sepsis and there was fluid in his lungs.

"The marks on my hands had turned from red to black – the sepsis was killing me," he said.

"The doctor said at the time that I was lucky to be alive but I was fighting for life."

Danny said he was diagnosed with endocarditis , a rare inflammation of the inner lining of the heart which is usually caused by an infection.

According to the NHS website, endocarditis usually happens when bacteria or fungus gets into the blood through the mouth or skin and travels to the heart - which was why Danny's pain initially appeared to be a toothache.

It says the most common symptoms are a high temperature, headache, feeling very tired, joint or muscle pain, night sweats, feeling breathless, loss of appetite, or losing weight without trying.

Sepsis is a serious, life-threatening reaction to an infection and can develop very quickly.

"They wanted to transfer me to Broadgreen Hospital in Liverpool but I wouldn't have survived the journey," said Danny.

He had to stay in hospital in Bangor until he was "strong enough" to make the trip, and underwent heart surgery in Liverpool on 6 July, which lasted six hours.

"My brother told me after that the operation was unsuccessful," he said.

"That was the first time the situation hit me on an emotional level and I felt really sad. I told my brother that I was tired of the whole thing, tired of fighting."

But, within a couple of days, a doctor told Danny that they had been given a special machine to help his blood clot properly, and they wanted to try the operation again.

It was successful the second time, with the infection cleared and the hole in the mitral valve closed.

After the operation, Danny was told he had suffered a series of strokes while in and out of consciousness.

"When the doctor was reading his notes afterwards, he said it was a miracle that I was still alive," said Danny, adding he had been told "the probability of survival was 1%".

Danny was transferred back to Ysbyty Gwynedd to begin his recovery.

"I couldn't walk at first, I didn't have the strength to do anything," he said.

But Danny said he saw progress after a couple of weeks, adding: "I walked with my daughter, Harriet, for the first time in months and that was very emotional.

"My family were a big part of my recovery and a big help as I fought through the whole thing. That's what got me through."

Danny was released from hospital on 19 August and says one of the first things he did was visit his dentist "because I knew he was very emotional about the situation".

"It wasn't his fault at all, my case and how it developed was something so rare," he said.

"I look after my teeth, clean them twice a day, so there's nothing I could have done differently. It's still a mystery to tell the truth.

"I had the worst possible scenario in my experience. Anyone can have toothache but, when endocarditis is part of it, that's when things change."

Danny said he was "extremely grateful" for all the support he had received in recent months.

"All the staff at Liverpool, Bangor – they've been amazing," he said.

"I'm meeting the surgeon from Broadgreen in Liverpool for the first time since the operation – that will be very emotional."

He added: "But Ceri made the first call, she was worried at first. If I had waited for another day or two, the story would have been very different.
